Here, we integrate single-cell DNA sequencing with surface proteomics to demonstrate that somatic TP53 mutations arise not only in leukemic blasts but also in T and NK cells from patients with TP53-mutant AML. TP53-mutant T cells exhibit enhanced exhaustion phenotypes, impaired cytotoxic function, and altered clonal architecture. Mechanistically, mutant p53 reprograms T cells toward a pro-inflammatory yet dysfunctional state, reshaping cytokine networks and promoting a niche enriched in inflammatory and myeloid-supportive signals. These mutant T cells impair both intrinsic effector function and the functionality of surrounding immune cells. Introduction of TP53 mutations into healthy donor T cells recapitulates exhaustion and impaired tumor control, whereas elimination of mutant p53 restores effector function, normalizes cytokine programs, and improves disease control in a TP53-mutant AML xenograft model.","gpl":"24676","gse":"324592","taxon":"Homo sapiens","entrytype":"GSE","gdstype":"Expression profiling by high throughput sequencing","ptechtype":"","valtype":"","ssinfo":"","subsetinfo":"","pdat":"2026/10/31","suppfile":"H5AD","samples":[{"accession":"GSM9579931","title":"T cells scRNAseq"},{"accession":"GSM9579932","title":"Monocyte scRNAseq"}],"relations":[],"extrelations":[],"n_samples":2,"seriestitle":"","platformtitle":"","platformtaxa":"","samplestaxa":"","pubmedids":[],"projects":[],"ftplink":"ftp://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/series/GSE324nnn/GSE324592/","geo2r":"no","bioproject":"PRJNA1435874"},"200305361":{"uid":"200305361","accession":"GSE305361","gds":"","title":"Disruption of nucleolar integrity triggers cellular quiescence through organelle rewiring and secretion","summary":"Intrinsic cellular stress responses are often mis regulated in complex human diseases such as cancer and neurodegeneration. To investigate how cellular homeostasis is balanced upon loss of key membraneless organelle – Nucleolus, we performed unbiased systems approach including cellular and temporal characterization of activated cellular stress signaling, associated sub-cellular changes and changes in cellular states and behavior. We report that transient loss of nucleolar architecture and defective ribosome biogenesis is well tolerated by cells as they undergo prolonged cell cycle arrest and rely on buffering capacity of cytoplasmic translation machinery. Cells immediately mount a comprehensive stress response predominantly mediated by TP53 and its downstream effector proteins. This mounted stress response is distinct from other acute stresses altering nucleolar morphology or function such as Pol I inhibition by ActD, heat shock or chemicals like Arsenate and CPT. Cells show a robust transcriptional reprogramming showing upregulation of structural and signaling genes of organelles such as Golgi apparatus and Endo-lysosomal vesicles. This leads to translation and microscopically evident tubular-vesicular expansion of Golgi and increase in number and size of endo-lysosomes. Cells become secretory, pro-metastatic and alter their cell-to-cell communication behavior. Taken together, these stress response pathways show an adaptive quiescent program and acquired partial EMT, allowing cells to resist loss of ribosome biogenesis, nucleolar architecture and ensure survival and restore homeostasis upon recovery. Correlatively, similar stress adaptions are seen to be contributing to progression of different cancer types especially in breast cancer and AML originating in the later stages of and Immune Profiling Characterizes Immune Heterogeneity and a TIGIT-Associated Subtype in Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma","summary":"Background and Aims: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) is characterised by marked molecular and microenvironmental heterogeneity and moderate response to immunotherapy. We aimed to define the genomic and spatial determinants of immune checkpoint activity in iCCA and their association with clinical outcome. Approach and Results: We performed integrated transcriptomic, DNA panel sequencing, and multiplex immunohistochemistry analyses in a cohort of 144 patients with iCCA. Tumors were classified according to STIM-defined microenvironmental subtypes. Spatially resolved immune profiling was conducted across tumor core, stroma, invasive margin, and adjacent liver. Immune checkpoint expression, cellular proximity, and clinical outcome were analysed using Cox regression and Kaplan-Meier methods. TIGIThigh tumors were further characterised by differential gene expression and pathway enrichment analyses. STIM classification stratified tumors into inflamed (47%) and non-inflamed (53%) subtypes with distinct survival outcomes and genomic profiles. Recurrent alterations in CDKN2A/B, TP53, MTAP, and BAP1 showed subtype-specific enrichment and prognostic relevance. Spatial immune profiling revealed compartment-specific distributions of T cells and immune checkpoints, with predominance of TIGIT and PD-1 expression in stromal and marginal regions. Most tumor-infiltrating T cells lacked inhibitory receptor expression, while co-expression of multiple checkpoints was uncommon. TIGIThigh tumors displayed coordinated activation of immune effector, antigen presentation, and interferon signalling pathways, alongside enrichment of distinct genomic alterations, defining an immune-activated molecular subtype. Conclusions: Integrated genomic and spatial immune profiling reveals pronounced context-dependent heterogeneity of immune checkpoint regulation in iCCA. TIGIT delineates an immune-activated subtype with distinct molecular features, providing a potential biomarker framework for patient stratification and rational immunotherapeutic degradation counteracts adaptation to androgen receptor inhibition in prostate cancer [RNA-seq]","summary":"The activation of androgen receptor (AR) signaling is the key lineage-specific oncogenic pathway and the primary therapeutic target in prostate cancer. While the therapeutic responses to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) and androgen receptor signaling inhibitors (ARSi) are highly variable, disease progression to fatal castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) is, in many cases, inevitable. The latter involves processes such as the reactivation of AR signaling, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and the transformation to AR-negative disease through lineage plasticity. In contrast, little is known about the early adaptation mechanisms in residual disease that initiate these processes, leading to tumor relapse. Here, we identify a critical role for TRIM24 in supporting the survival of residual cancer cell subpopulations primed for tumor relapse in vivo. In agreement, the reduction of TRIM24 through bi-functional degraders (dTRIM24) significantly delays or abrogates the emergence of CRPC related to AR-reactivation and lineage plasticity. Mechanistically, dTRIM24 inhibits AR/mTOR signaling in residual disease but, more importantly, also counteracts adaptive pathways directly engaged by AR inhibition, such as STAT3-signaling and the release of EMT-promoting cytokines. Finally, dTRIM24’s anti-tumor activity also extends to CPRC models with limited therapeutic options. In summary, the findings more broadly position TRIM24 as an effective and druggable target for preventing prostate cancer progression under AR inhibition.","gpl":"18573","gse":"267345","taxon":"Homo
